lesson.title: A Level Playing Field: Standard Enthalpy Conditions
lesson.summary: Standard enthalpy, denoted with the degree symbol as delta H degree, is an enthalpy change measured under an agreed set of standard state conditions, so that values reported by different experiments and different labs can be fairly compared and combined.
lesson.body:
An enthalpy change is not a fixed constant of nature the way, say, the charge of an electron is. It depends on the physical state, pressure, and concentration of every reactant and product involved. Water as a gas has a different enthalpy than water as a liquid; a gas at high pressure has a different enthalpy than the same gas at low pressure. Without some agreed reference point, a delta H measured in one lab could not be meaningfully compared to, or combined with, a delta H measured in another lab under different conditions. Chemists solved this by defining standard states: gases are considered standard at a pressure of 1 bar, solutes in solution are standard at a concentration of 1 M, and pure solids and liquids are standard in their most stable form at that pressure. Elements are standard in whatever physical form is most stable, such as graphite for carbon or diatomic O2 gas for oxygen. Any enthalpy value measured under these conditions is marked with a degree symbol, delta H degree, read as delta H standard, or standard enthalpy.

Temperature is handled slightly differently. It is not technically part of the definition of a standard state, but because enthalpy values do shift somewhat with temperature, chemists needed a conventional reference temperature anyway, and 25 degrees C, that is, 298 K, became the standard choice for published tables of thermodynamic data. Unless a different temperature is explicitly stated, you can assume any delta H degree value you encounter was measured, or is reported as if measured, at 25 degrees C.

This matters practically because an ordinary calorimetry experiment run at room temperature and normal atmospheric pressure, essentially what a coffee cup calorimeter does by default, already approximates standard conditions reasonably well. That means a student's own carefully run calorimetry results can be legitimately compared against, or treated as an estimate of, the standard enthalpy values published in reference tables.

Take the neutralization of 25.0 mL of 2.00 M HCl with 25.0 mL of 2.00 M NaOH inside a coffee cup calorimeter, both solutions starting at 25.0 degrees C, approximately standard temperature. The final temperature after mixing is 38.6 degrees C, so delta T = 38.6 minus 25.0 = 13.6 degrees C. Assuming the combined 50.0 mL solution has a mass of 50.0 g and a specific heat capacity of 4.18 J/(g times degree C), the heat absorbed by the solution is q = m c delta T = (50.0 g)(4.18 J/(g times degree C))(13.6 degrees C) = (209.0 J/degree C)(13.6 degrees C) = 2,842.4 J, or 2.84 kJ. Since this heat was released by the neutralization reaction, q(reaction) = negative 2.84 kJ, and because the reaction ran at constant atmospheric pressure and near standard temperature, this equals delta H degree for the amount reacted. There are (0.0250 L)(2.00 mol/L) = 0.0500 mol of HCl, matched exactly by 0.0500 mol of NaOH, so delta H degree = negative 2.84 kJ divided by 0.0500 mol = negative 56.8 kJ/mol, a standard enthalpy of neutralization consistent with values found in reference tables for strong acid, strong base reactions.
